title: BETWEEN
description: Use SQL BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN with inclusive endpoints, NULL and reversed bounds; compare closed ranges with half-open date and time windows.
notes:
## A closed interval includes both boundaries

BETWEEN tests whether a value falls within an inclusive interval. If an equipment budget admits prices from two hundred through six hundred, a price of exactly two hundred qualifies and a price of exactly six hundred also qualifies. The operator is a concise way to express those two inclusive comparisons when the operands have a suitable shared comparison domain.

Translate the requirement before choosing the syntax. Everyday language can use between loosely, sometimes implying that endpoints are excluded. SQL does not infer that intention. If a rule requires strictly more than two hundred and strictly less than six hundred, write the corresponding strict comparisons instead. The convenient keyword should follow the business interval rather than redefine it.

## Read the three operands deliberately

The tested value comes first, then the lower bound, then the upper bound. For correctly typed numeric values, the condition means the value is at least the lower bound and at most the upper bound. The AND inside BETWEEN connects its two bounds; it does not introduce an unrelated independent eligibility condition. A later AND can combine the whole interval predicate with another requirement.

For example, quantity between two and six can be combined with a known equipment category. Both interval endpoints remain included. Parentheses around the interval are optional in many simple forms but can improve readability in compound logic. When a condition contains several ranges and alternatives, group the policy explicitly so a category exception does not accidentally bypass the quantity restriction.

```sql
SELECT request_id, quantity
FROM equipment_requests
WHERE quantity BETWEEN 2 AND 6
ORDER BY request_id;
```

## Equal bounds describe one value

An interval whose lower and upper bounds are both four is valid. For ordinary known comparable values, it admits exactly four. It is an unusual way to express equality but demonstrates that inclusiveness is meaningful even when an interval has zero width. Do not reject equal bounds merely because an interface label suggests the minimum and maximum must always differ.

Reversed bounds have different semantics. For known numeric values, a lower bound of six and an upper bound of two produces no qualifying value under ordinary BETWEEN. MySQL does not automatically swap the supplied bounds. An interface may choose to reject a reversed request or normalize it under an explicit contract, but that is an application decision before SQL is constructed.

## Unknown operands need three-valued reasoning

A [NULL](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/null-values) tested value does not satisfy an ordinary known numeric range in WHERE. With known non-NULL bounds, its comparisons are unknown and the combined result is UNKNOWN. WHERE excludes it. If missing quantities belong in an investigation report, add a deliberate IS NULL branch instead of assume BETWEEN treats absence as zero or an unbounded value.

NULL bounds need additional care. A compound interval can be FALSE when one comparison is definitely false even if the other is unknown. Do not memorize the blanket claim that any NULL anywhere always forces every BETWEEN expression to UNKNOWN. Analyze the logical comparisons under the actual type rules. The exercises keep bounds known so their missing-value policy remains straightforward and testable.

## Negating the interval keeps endpoints out

NOT BETWEEN describes values outside the closed interval when the operands are known and comparably typed. For two through six, quantities below two or above six qualify. Quantities exactly two and six are inside the original interval and therefore excluded by the negated predicate. A NULL quantity still does not become a known outside value simply because the predicate is negated.

If an exception report needs both outside values and missing measurements, combine NOT BETWEEN with IS NULL. Keep that choice explicit in the report description. Confirmed out-of-range data and absent data can require different correction actions, so returning a classification alongside the identity may be more useful than collapsing them into one unexplained invalid category.

## Calendar dates and instants have different boundaries

A [DATE](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/data-types) interval can express a closed range of calendar dates. When the stored value includes a time, a date-only literal used as an upper bound can represent midnight at the beginning of that date. An inclusive comparison then admits that instant but may exclude the rest of the same calendar day. The SQL is following its operands, even if the English requirement intended the entire day.

This is a frequent source of missing end-of-month records. A range from the first day through the thirty-first, written using date-only endpoints against DATETIME, does not necessarily include an event at noon on the thirty-first. Test midnight, midday and a fractional time on the final date. Those cases reveal a boundary problem that examples using only the first day never expose.

## Half-open time windows avoid invented end instants

For a whole calendar month of timestamp-like values, an inclusive start and exclusive next-month start often communicates the intent more robustly. The comparison admits every representable time before the next boundary without selecting an artificial final second. It also remains understandable if the column's fractional precision changes. BETWEEN is not required merely because the requirement describes a time range.

```sql
SELECT event_id, occurred_at
FROM inventory_events
WHERE occurred_at >= '2026-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND occurred_at < '2026-02-01 00:00:00'
ORDER BY event_id;
```

State which time zone defines the month. TIMESTAMP interpretation can depend on session time-zone settings, while DATETIME has different storage semantics. A campus-local reporting month and a UTC month can select different instants. A fixed synthetic DATETIME exercise can isolate interval reasoning, but it does not establish a production time-zone conversion policy for every event source.

## Comparable text still follows collation

BETWEEN can compare text, but the range follows text comparison semantics rather than a human category list. Labels between Camera and Tripod do not mean only those two categories. Other strings may fall within the interval according to their collation. Use IN for an explicit list of permitted categories; use a text range only when that ordering actually defines the requirement.

Collation can affect case, accent and padding comparisons. Numeric-looking text can also order differently from numeric quantities, and mixing operand types may trigger conversion. Align the tested value and bounds with the intended domain. Avoid claiming that every string range behaves identically across schemas or that quoting numeric bounds always preserves the intended numeric comparison.

## Bound parameters still require a contract

A search endpoint should validate the supplied minimum and maximum, choose the intended types and decide what missing bounds mean. One-sided filtering may be supported, but it needs explicit construction such as a lower-bound comparison without an upper bound. Passing NULL to BETWEEN is not an automatic way to express an open-ended interval.

Bind accepted values using the client's supported parameter mechanism. Do not concatenate untrusted bounds into SQL text. Binding protects representation but does not resolve a reversed interval, select the time zone or authorize access to the underlying rows. Those responsibilities stay at their trusted boundaries, and the query applies the requested range only within the permitted data scope.

## Test adjacent intervals and exact boundaries

Closed intervals that share an endpoint both include that endpoint. Two adjacent time reports using inclusive January-end and inclusive February-start bounds can overlap if the endpoint is the same instant. Half-open intervals with a shared boundary admit that instant only in the later interval. Choose interval shapes that match whether overlap is allowed and whether every event must belong to exactly one reporting period.

The first exercise preserves the existing Mid-Range Prices identity, schema and sample, adding fixtures at both price endpoints. The second selects a full month of DATETIME events using an explicit half-open window. Both include near-boundary alternatives and missing values. Explain each included and excluded event in terms of its exact value, then confirm that the final ordering is deterministic and independent of how the database physically retrieves the matching rows.


The retained price band uses two hundred and one thousand, while the earlier quantity example uses two and six. The numeric values differ, but both are closed intervals. Follow each task’s stated operands rather than copy bounds from a nearby illustration. A correct reference solution preserves the original product properties and ordered output while testing the requested price domain.

questions.question_text: Does ordinary numeric BETWEEN include its endpoints?
options: Yes, both lower and upper endpoints
questions.explanation: It describes a closed interval.

questions.question_text: Which explicit numeric condition matches quantity BETWEEN 2 AND 6?
questions.explanation: Both inclusive comparisons must hold.

questions.question_text: Can BETWEEN be used with suitably typed dates?
options: Yes, the values use their comparison semantics
Only with a separate RANGE keyword
questions.explanation: Temporal boundaries still need precise interpretation.

questions.question_text: For known numeric bounds, what does BETWEEN 6 AND 2 do?
options: No known numeric value can satisfy the reversed interval
questions.explanation: MySQL ordinary BETWEEN does not normalize reversed input.

questions.question_text: Why can a date-only final-day bound miss DATETIME events?
options: It can represent midnight at the beginning of that day
It always becomes the next month
questions.explanation: Later times on the same calendar date can exceed the bound.

questions.question_text: For known quantity, what does NOT BETWEEN 2 AND 6 admit?
options: Only values strictly inside the interval
questions.explanation: The original endpoints remain inside and are excluded by negation.

questions.question_text: What does BETWEEN 4 AND 4 admit for known numeric values?
questions.explanation: Equal inclusive bounds define a valid singleton interval.

questions.question_text: Why translate everyday uses of between carefully?
options: SQL always guesses the intended endpoints
The intended endpoint policy may differ from SQL inclusiveness
questions.explanation: The requirement must specify endpoint meaning.

questions.question_text: Does a NULL quantity qualify for a known numeric BETWEEN range in WHERE?
options: Yes, it becomes the lower bound
questions.explanation: WHERE retains only TRUE.

questions.question_text: Does NOT BETWEEN automatically include NULL quantities?
options: Yes, every missing value is outside
No, negation does not make an unknown range result true
questions.explanation: Add an explicit missingness branch when the contract requires it.

questions.question_text: What expresses January as a full DATETIME month?
options: Between January 1 and January 31 midnight only
At or after January 1 and strictly before February 1
questions.explanation: The half-open interval includes all final-day times.

questions.question_text: Why avoid an invented last fractional instant of a day?
options: Every last second is always identical
The next exclusive boundary avoids dependence on column precision
A time range needs only one bound
questions.explanation: Use a robust interval shape for timestamp-like values.

questions.question_text: What should an API do with reversed numeric bounds?
questions.explanation: Normalization is an application decision.

questions.question_text: How should a missing maximum be represented in an open-ended search?
options: Build the supported one-sided condition deliberately
Pass NULL as an unlimited upper bound
Use a random large number without a contract
questions.explanation: NULL is not automatically positive infinity.

questions.question_text: Why is text BETWEEN not a substitute for two named allowed categories?
options: It always means exactly the two endpoints
It admits an ordering interval, potentially including other strings
It always converts labels to dates
questions.explanation: Use explicit membership for a category list.

questions.question_text: What can affect text interval membership?
options: Only the file encoding of the SQL comment
questions.explanation: Comparison semantics determine ordering.

questions.question_text: Two closed intervals share the same endpoint. What can happen?
options: The database raises an overlap error
That endpoint belongs to both intervals
questions.explanation: Use half-open periods if exclusive membership is required.

questions.question_text: What should define a reporting month for TIMESTAMP data?
options: The intended time zone and interval boundaries
questions.explanation: Different zones can describe different instants.

questions.question_text: Does any NULL operand force every BETWEEN expression to UNKNOWN in all cases?
options: No, a definite false comparison can determine the conjunction
No, NULL is always greater than everything
questions.explanation: Analyze the underlying logic rather than use a blanket rule.

questions.question_text: Which fixture exposes a mistaken exclusive endpoint?
options: A quantity exactly equal to the lower or upper bound
questions.explanation: Boundary rows distinguish inclusive from strict comparisons.

coding_problems.title: Mid-Range Prices
coding_problems.task: Return id,name,price for products priced from 200 through 1000 inclusive, ordered by id. Preserve the original required-price schema and do not add category or stock conditions.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  category TEXT NOT NULL,
  price INTEGER NOT NULL,
  stock INTEGER
);
coding_problems.seed_sql:
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, stock) VALUES
(1, 'ProLaptop', 'Electronics', 85000, 12),
(2, 'Notebook', 'Stationery', 40, NULL),
(3, 'Python Basics', 'Books', 350, 5),
(4, 'ProPhone', 'Electronics', 45000, 0),
(5, 'Novel', 'Books', 220, NULL),
(6, 'Desk Lamp', 'Home', 900, 8);
coding_problems.expected:
id	name	price
3	Python Basics	350
5	Novel	220
6	Desk Lamp	900
coding_problems.ordering: As explicitly ordered in the result query.
constraints: Use only the supplied synthetic tables and requested transition.
hints: Keep all original output roles and id ordering.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT id,name,price FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 200 AND 1000 ORDER BY id;
coding_problems.explanation: The closed interval includes exactly 200 and 1000. Category and stock do not restrict this retained requirement.

validation_cases.seed_sql:
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, stock) VALUES
(1, 'ProTablet', 'Electronics', 32000, 4),
(2, 'Pencil Set', 'Stationery', 60, NULL),
(3, 'SQL Guide', 'Books', 500, 10),
(4, 'ProSpeaker', 'Electronics', 6000, 0);

coding_problems.title: Capture a full DATETIME month
coding_problems.task: Return event_id for every non-NULL occurred_at in January 2026. Use an inclusive January 1 boundary and an exclusive February 1 boundary. occurred_at is a synthetic DATETIME(6), with no time-zone conversion in this task. Order by event_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE inventory_events(event_id INT PRIMARY KEY,occurred_at DATETIME(6));
coding_problems.ordering: As explicitly ordered in the result query.
constraints: Use only the supplied synthetic tables and requested transition.
edge_cases: A fractional instant on the final day qualifies.
The first February instant does not qualify.
hints: Do not use January 31 midnight as the final-day ceiling.
Filter before February 1 rather than guess the last second.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT event_id FROM inventory_events WHERE occurred_at>='2026-01-01 00:00:00' AND occurred_at<'2026-02-01 00:00:00' ORDER BY event_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The next-month exclusive bound includes every representable January time and excludes February midnight without an artificial final fractional instant.

original_questions.question_text: Is BETWEEN inclusive or exclusive of its endpoints?
options: Inclusive of the lower bound only
Inclusive of the upper bound only
original_questions.explanation: BETWEEN low AND high includes both low and high themselves.

original_questions.question_text: Which expression is exactly equivalent to `price BETWEEN 200 AND 1000`?
original_questions.explanation: BETWEEN is shorthand for the inclusive >= and <= combination.

original_questions.question_text: Can BETWEEN be used with date or string values, not just numbers?
options: No, only numeric types are supported
Yes — BETWEEN works on any comparable type, including dates and strings
Only with the DATE type specifically
BETWEEN requires exactly two numeric arguments
original_questions.explanation: BETWEEN applies to any type that supports ordering comparisons.

original_questions.question_text: What happens if the low value in BETWEEN is greater than the high value?
options: It silently matches zero rows, since no value can satisfy both conditions
It automatically swaps the two values
original_questions.explanation: A reversed range simply can never be satisfied, so the result is empty rather than an error.

original_questions.question_text: What is a subtle risk of using `order_date BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31'` on a TIMESTAMP column?
options: No risk — this always captures the entire month correctly
'2026-01-31' implies midnight at the start of that day, so timestamps later on the 31st could be excluded
BETWEEN cannot be used with TIMESTAMP columns at all
This syntax causes a guaranteed error
original_questions.explanation: The implicit midnight boundary on the upper date can silently exclude part of the intended day.

original_questions.question_text: What does NOT BETWEEN 200 AND 1000 match?
options: Values strictly less than 200 or strictly greater than 1000 (200 and 1000 themselves are excluded from the match)
original_questions.explanation: NOT BETWEEN inverts the inclusive range, excluding the boundary values themselves from the negated match.

original_questions.question_text: Is `age BETWEEN 18 AND 18` a valid, meaningful condition?
options: Yes — it is equivalent to age = 18, just an unusual way to write it
BETWEEN requires the two bounds to differ
original_questions.explanation: Using the same value for both bounds is valid and equivalent to an equality check.

original_questions.question_text: How is 'between' in everyday English different from SQL's BETWEEN, that's worth being careful about?
options: There is no difference at all
Everyday English sometimes implies an exclusive range, while SQL's BETWEEN is always inclusive of both endpoints
SQL's BETWEEN is exclusive, unlike everyday English
Everyday English BETWEEN only applies to numbers
original_questions.explanation: This mismatch in intuition is exactly why BETWEEN's inclusive-both-ends behavior is worth stating explicitly.
